25%–50% of children aged 1–5 years will remain chronically 
infected with HBV.26 In contrast, approximately 95% of adults
recover completely from HBV infection and do not become 
chronically infected. Asian Americans and Native Hawaiian
and other Paciﬁ c Islanders have the highest rates of chronic
hepatitis B among all racial/ethnic groups in the United States
and also a disproportionately high risk for liver cancer. Most
Asian Americans are infected with HBV as infants or children.
Th e HBV infection-related death rate among Asian Americans
and Native Hawaiians and Other Paciﬁ c Islanders is seven 
times greater than the rate among whites.27
Th ere are several diﬀ erent blood tests available to diagnose hepa-
titis B (see Box 16.3) and monitor treatment. For acute infection,
no medication is available; treatment is supportive, much like that 
for HAV. For chronic infection, several antiviral drugs (adefovir
dipivoxil, interferon alfa-2b, pegylated interferon alfa-2a, lamivu-
dine, entecavir, and telbivudine) are available. (Table 16.5 provides
